content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors create neural network models with architectures based on the full connectome of *C. elegans* in order to ascertain whether it confers useful priors for ANN applications.  The authors demonstrate that, using weight parameters learned via genetic algorithms, both the specific and an abstracted architecture can outperform more traditional MLP networks of similar sizes when employed on a swimming task that approximates the crawling motor task that the *C. elegans* connectome evolved to optimize.  Conversely, they show that the architecture is substantially sub-optimal compared to traditional MLP networks for tasks that materially differ from such crawling behaviors: quadrupedal locomotion and MNIST digit recognition.  These results serve as a proof of principle that, at least in certain circumstances, connectomes might assist ML researchers in desigining optimal, efficient architectures.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The authors model the full connectome of *C. elegans*, using 3 different neuronal models that differ in their biophysical realism, suggesting that the connectome, rather than the particular neural model chosen, is key to the performance improvements that are documented

2. The authors demonstrate counterfactual examples, showing that connectomes can be narrowly optimized for specific tasks

Weaknesses:

Major:

1. The main thrust of the present work--that biological connectomes can provide useful priors for ML applications--is demonstrated in the referenced Bhattasali et al. 2022 manuscript. While the authors here provide additional insights, including that the precise connectome can substantively improve performance over a coarse approximation of the connectome, they represent minor advances over Bhattasali.  

2. While the authors demonstrate that the connectome-informed architecture can outperform traditional MLP architectures, they do so using an inefficient training regimen (genetic algorithms).  While such a demonstration is interesting, further analyses demonstrating the same results for more state-of-the art training protocols, such as deep RL methods, would be needed for ML researchers to compare the various networks' performances.  Cf. Bhattasali, in which such comparisons are done.  Apropos, the average rewards documented there are ~1,000, $\geq$4x more than the "average performance" reported in the present work (presumably these metrics are the same; see below).  

3. Similarly, while the authors mention an "ideal solution" (p. 4), it is neither described (e.g., is it qualitatively different from what is achieved here?) nor compared to the performance attained by the various models.  Similarly for the cheetah performance

4. The description of how the authors mapped the circuits of the connectome to their network is extraordinarily terse, making it difficult to understand or replicate. While the software tool that will be provided can help, much more detail is needed here. Cf. Bhattasali et al.'s much more detailed explanation of their model

Minor:

1. "Average performance" is left undefined.  If this is the same as "average reward," the more common, latter term should be used.  Otherwise, the term should be defined.  In either scenario, no intuition is given for how this should be interpreted.  Moreover, no demonstration (e.g., figures, videos) are provided so that the reader can readily interpret what an average performance matching those in Figs. 3-4 corresponds to.

2. In Fig. 3, the results are cut off at a time where it appears only the Izhikevich model has plateaued. If the artificial and adaptive LIF networks reach a higher performance than the Izhikevich model, this should be shown and discussed.

3. The Evolutionary Strategies algorithm is not described at all (beyond the hyperparameters used)

4. The x-axes of Figs. 3-4 are not uniform, varying in whether they represent time steps or epochs.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The present work adds some results--including null results--to the results reported in the referenced Bhattasali paper; however, the advances are minor and insufficiently explored.  The mappings of the connectome to the presented models are described too briefly, and the actual model performances--aside from MNIST--are not well characterized (i.e., what does an average performance of 250 mean?).
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors model networks based off of the connectome of *C. elegans*. While they show that, under the circumstances studied, the architecture can serve as a valuable prior in applications sufficiently similar to those served by the biological network, Bhattasali et al. 2022 have already demonstrated this.  Moreover, the circumstances studied here--i.e., training the network weights by genetic algorithm--while of interest, do not represent ideal circumstances of interest to ML applications. When more advanced RL algorithms are used, Bhattasali et al. seem to have attained much higher performance (if "performance" here is the same as "reward" in the Bhattasali paper).  The model explanation is also curtailed, making it difficult to understand the implementation without resorting to reading through the code.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper addresses an important question that is can we extract information (mostly structural) from connectomics data in order to build better machine learning models? 

The authors propose using the C. Elegans connectome to inform/bias the neural network design. The main claim is that bias from connectomes (only a few being available as of today) could help inform the design of neural networks and design of machine learning models. 

The authors propose to evaluate the resulting model on two locomotive tasks, which is what C.Elegans does in the wild, and one less related, and a visual task, which is totally unrelated. Testing the model on a visual task is relevant because it is not what the C Elegans has evolved to do, and thus would possibly confirm the bias assumption. 

The results show that for the first task (the locomotion of C.Elegans) indeed the connectome-inspired model does perform best but not for the other two tasks, although one is still a locomotion task.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well-written and gives an excellent introduction to C.Elegans as a model organism for studying the combination of ML and Neuroscience. 

The paper, however, falls short in many aspects. First, the main is not supported as it is not clear at all that the connectome is optimal for the task at hand, even the one that C.Elegans has evolved to do. Many other factors could affect the resulting connectome. As a result, the experiment does not validate the claim. 

Furthermore, the performance on the other locomotion task is poor, "similarly" to the visual task. As a result, the conclusion is that one would not be able to generalize to other tasks with the connectome. This contradicts the possibility of re-routing various cortical areas, for example, auditory and visual in Ferrets and style have a fully functioning organism. 

It is also not clear how genetic encoding of neural architecture and plasticity would be different between Mammals and worms (or insects like flies) for which parts of the connectome are known. Authors of other works, from approaches more normative, have shown that the same plasticity rules and underlying rules lead to neural circuits that are adapted to the type of organisms. 

It is thus not clear how the authors relate to other work cited in the conclusion, which shows that architectural search and plasticity allow for generalizing models.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clear and well-written. 
The paper lack novelties and the main claim is not supported or in contradiction to the dogma of plasticity.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper addresses an important question that could greatly benefit the Neuroscience and ML communities. However, the paper makes claims that are not supported and draws conclusions without providing compelling evidence. 
I believe that the question is important and encourage the authors to further the research, but the current paper falls short in many aspects.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper tests how the C. elegans locomotion circuit motif and its statistics can be applied to the solution of a task similar to that solved by the circuit (Swimmer) and to two unrelated tasks (half cheetah, MNIST classification). Experiments show that the simulated neural circuit trained with a genetic algorithm works well regardless of the complexity of the neuron model used, with more complex models training more quickly, and that 2-layer MLPs with sparsity and e:i ratio of the connectome work better than fully connected MLPs or MLPs with random sparse connectivity.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths of the paper include a setup simplified relative to prior work (no use of an oscillator), and the evaluation of the derived networks on problems other than Swimmer (where the connectome constraints did not provide a beneficial effect).

Weaknesses include incomplete information for an independent reproduction of the results -- for instance, the total number of parameters in the MLP layers is not stated anywhere, the specific e:i ratios are not quoted, etc (see below for more). The experimental results are also limited to only three specific scenarios. A more complete exploration of how the various factors of number of free parameters, e:i ratio, number of nonlinearities, sparsity rate would be significantly more informative here.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper provides a very useful and clear short overview of the relevant C. elegans biology and single neuron models. The idea of using this specific C. elegans circuit in the context of an artificial network was proposed in prior work (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.05242.pdf), which the authors of the current paper cite. The implementation of the circuit and how it's applied to the Swimmer task in the current paper is novel, and the differences to prior work are highlighted in the text.

The authors mention software for converting connectome information into artificial networks, including information from other organisms (Drosophila). However, the software is not made available during review, and is not described in the text, so it cannot be evaluated.

The hyperparameters of the algorithms used are listed in the appendix. It is also only the appendix that explains that a pretrained non-linear encoder is used for the inputs and outputs of the networks. The details of the encoder are not given. Similarly, the appendix also explains that all weights were pretrained with ES prior to GA optimization. The clarity of the paper would be improved by explaining these details in the main text.

The GA optimization used in the paper was tuned to reflect conditions of natural C. elegans populations (population size, single-parent children). This added biological realism seems misplaced -- the real worm does not optimize the same reward function, and the parameters of the network might not be under strict genetic control (see e.g. doi:10.1038/s41586-021-03778-8)

Comments:
* In Fig. 1, the dorsal/ventral labels for the muscle cells/body walls seem inverted relative to location of the DB / VB cells (see e.g. Sengupta & Samuel (2009))
* "[...] connectome statistics since outside of the C. elegans this constitutes the majority of our knowledge of the connectomes of other organisms"; this understates the amount of connectomic information available. For instance, there are now reconstructions of significant parts of the Drosophila brain, as well as cutouts of various sizes of vertebrate brains.
* In Fig. 3. The caption "Performance across" is incomplete.
* In Fig. 4. What are the confidence intervals computed over?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents some interesting first steps in how to use connectome information in a machine learning setting. The experimental results are restricted to a very specific and limited problem (locomotion through an oscillation of the body). The results seem to imply that sparsity and the e:i ratio are useful priors for training artificial networks solving problems similar to those solved by the original circuit in nature. This is an interesting result, and in line with prior work in Bhattasali et al. (2022). Unfortunately, the experimental part of the paper is not extensive enough to be able to convince the reader whether this could be a more general rule, or is something very specific to the investigated setup. The setting with the swimmer task used here appears also simple enough that one could attempt an analysis of what it is mechanistically that allows the C elegans-constrained MLP to learn better. Overall, this paper continues to advance an interesting line of research, but seems to take a bit too small a step towards new territory.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper has discussed how biological connectomes can be used in machine learning problems to improve the learning efficiency over general dense networks. This paper extracts statistics of the connectome of C. Elegans to inspire the design of a neural network. For a swimmer agent, this biologically-inspired neural network has shown much better learning efficiency than a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). In contrary, for tasks like image classification or legged locomotion, the biologically-inspired neural network becomes much less efficient than a MLP. As a result, this paper has concluded that biological connectomes provide benefits for machine learning problems only under appropriate task scenarios.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The paper is well written and the presentation is clear.
2. It's interesting to inspire the design of neural networks from biological neural networks. Such design might be beneficial for understanding functions of biological neural networks.
3. It is shown that only statistics of the connectome of an organism are required to improve the task performance over a MLP. It shows the possibility to extract statistics of the connectome of higher animals to design neural networks that can solve more complex problems efficiently.

Weaknesses: 
1. The behavior of C. Elegans is unfortunately too simple to show higher-level brain functions other than simple locomotions.
2. The experiments are relatively sparse. How the performance shown in Figure 4 varies when hyper-parameters change? Whether the improvement over MLPs is robust enough?
3. Authors have mentioned that many the statistics of the connectome of many organisms are already applicable. Whether the connectome of other organisms can improve the performance over MLP similarly?
4. A detailed elaboration of each biological neuron models seems unnecessary and contributes little to the main theme of this paper. I suggest to reduce this part for increasing performance comparisons with MLPs, under different conditions.
5. Any discussions about the reason why the connectome of C. Elegans can learn locomotion more efficiently than MLPs?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is clearly written and the quality is good. The proposed method is valid and the novelty of this paper is good. The experiments in this paper are reproducible and the codes of the software will be made publicly available.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the connectome and behavior of C. Elegans are relatively simple, it's still interesting to inspire the design of neural networks from biological connectomes. My major concern is the performance improvement in Figure 4 might not be robust across different hyper-parameters or experimental conditions. It's good to show the performance improvement can persist for statistics of connectomes in other organisms.

content.title: Biological connectomes as a representation for the architecture of artificial neural networks
content.TL;DR: We map the neural circuitry of a nematode taken from neuroscience literature into an ANN and show that it works well on certain tasks but not others.
content.abstract: Grand efforts in neuroscience are working toward mapping the connectomes of many new species, including the near completion of the Drosophila melanogaster. It is important to ask whether these models could benefit artificial intelligence. In this work we ask two fundamental questions: (1) where and when biological connectomes can provide use in machine learning, (2) which design principles are necessary for extracting a good representation of the connectome. Toward this end, we translate the motor circuit of the C. Elegans nematode into artificial neural networks at varying levels of biophysical realism and evaluate the outcome of training these networks on motor and non-motor behavioral tasks. We demonstrate that biophysical realism need not be upheld to attain the advantages of using biological circuits. We also establish that, even if the exact wiring diagram is not retained, the architectural statistics provide a valuable prior. Finally, we show that while the C. Elegans locomotion circuit provides a powerful inductive bias on locomotion problems, its structure may hinder performance on tasks unrelated to locomotion such as visual classification problems.
